stem: A platform team keeps its build commands, review checklist, and naming conventions in a Claude Code instruction file. The guidance must reach everyone who clones the payments-api repository, travel with that repository in version control, and have no effect when the same developers work in their other repositories. Where should the file live?

options.text: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on each developer's machine, kept in step across the team by hand
CLAUDE.md at the repository root, or .claude/CLAUDE.md, committed to the repository
CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root, listed in .gitignore so it stays out of commits
A managed-policy CLAUDE.md deployed by IT to the operating system's system-wide location

explanation: Project scope is the only scope that is both repository-bound and shareable through source control. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md from the working directory and every directory above it at launch, so a file committed at the repository root reaches every clone of that repository and nothing else. Project instructions are where build and test commands, coding standards, architectural decisions, and common workflows belong, because those are the things a new teammate would otherwise have to be told.

distractorNotes.a: This is user scope: it applies to one person across every project on that machine, and it cannot be version-controlled alongside the repository.
distractorNotes.c: This is local scope: personal, project-specific preferences that are deliberately gitignored, so teammates never receive them.
distractorNotes.d: Managed policy is organization-wide and applies in every repository. It also requires IT or device-management deployment, which is far broader than one repository's conventions.

sourceNote: Section "Choose where to put CLAUDE.md files": project instructions live at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, are for "Team-shared instructions for the project", and are "Shared with: Team members via source control". The same table scopes ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to "Just you (all projects)", ./CLAUDE.local.md to "Just you (current project)" with the advice to add it to .gitignore, and managed policy files to "All users in organization". Section "How CLAUDE.md files load" states that Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md "from your current working directory and every directory above it".

stem: A security team must guarantee that one Claude Code setting holds on every machine and cannot be changed by any developer. Separately, a developer wants a personal override for one project that is never committed to the repository. Select TWO statements that correctly describe how the configuration layers serve these two needs.

options.text: User-level configuration is the strongest of the layers a developer controls, because it describes the person rather than any particular project.
Configuration distributed centrally by the organisation cannot be overridden by any file a developer controls, which is what makes it fit for policy.
A key set at more than one layer is reported as a conflict at startup and ignored everywhere until someone removes the duplicate definitions.
Among the layers a developer controls, the more specific and local one wins, so an uncommitted personal file overrides the shared project file.
A value supplied for a single session is the weakest layer of all, so any configuration file present on disk will override it at run time.

explanation: The layers are ordered so that the two needs do not compete. Configuration an organisation distributes sits above everything an individual can edit, so it is the only layer that can carry a guarantee; anything a developer can edit, a developer can undo. Below that, precedence runs from the general to the specific, so a personal file scoped to one project beats the shared project file, which in turn beats the developer's global preferences. That ordering is what lets a personal override exist without weakening the policy above it.

distractorNotes.a: Inverts the developer-controlled ordering. User-level settings are the broadest and most general of them, so they are overridden by project and project-local files rather than winning over them.
distractorNotes.c: Setting a key at several layers is the normal case that precedence exists to resolve, not an error state. Refusing to apply the key would make layered configuration unusable.
distractorNotes.e: Reverses the relationship. A value supplied for one session is the most specific expression of intent available, so it sits above the files on disk rather than beneath them.

sourceNote: Settings precedence figure, highest to lowest: 1. Managed settings (managed-settings.json, MDM, or the claude.ai console), 2. Command line (claude --settings), 3. Project local (.claude/settings.local.json), 4. Shared project (.claude/settings.json), 5. User (~/.claude/settings.json), summarized as "A key set at a higher level overrides the same key set lower down." The page's "Settings files and who they affect" table gives the scope of each file.

stem: A team runs Claude Code fully unattended inside a container with --dangerously-skip-permissions, which puts the session in bypassPermissions mode. Their security reviewer asks which of the permission rules configured in the repository's settings still have any force. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both deny and allow rules stop applying, because bypassPermissions skips the permission system in its entirety.
Allow rules keep pre-approving the tools they name, but deny rules are relaxed so the session can run without stopping.
Deny rules apply only until the first prompt would have been shown, after which the mode suppresses them for the rest of the session.
Deny rules still block in every mode, including bypassPermissions, while allow rules have no effect in that mode.

explanation: Permission modes set the baseline for what runs without asking, and permission rules layer on top of that baseline rather than being replaced by it. Deny rules are the part that survives everywhere: they block in every mode, bypassPermissions included, which is what makes a deny rule a dependable control rather than a convenience default. Allow rules are the mirror image and have no effect in bypassPermissions, because nothing there needs pre-approving. A short list of actions is auto-approved by no mode at all, including tools matched by an explicit ask rule, tools that require user interaction such as AskUserQuestion, and rm or rmdir removals targeting a critical path; in a -p run those few calls are denied rather than prompted. None of this makes the mode safe on its own, which is why it is documented as requiring a container, VM, or sandbox runtime.

distractorNotes.a: The mode skips the permission prompts, not the rule set. Deny rules are explicitly carved out as applying in every mode, and a handful of actions are auto-approved by no mode whatsoever.
distractorNotes.b: This inverts both halves. Allow rules are the ones rendered inert, since there is nothing left to pre-approve, and deny rules are the ones that keep applying.
distractorNotes.c: There is no first-prompt threshold. Deny rules are evaluated on every matching call for the whole session regardless of mode.

sourceNote: Section "Available modes": "Modes set the baseline. Layer permission rules on top to pre-approve or block specific tools. Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions... Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions." The carve-outs are listed under "Actions no mode auto-approves" (explicit ask rules, tools requiring user interaction such as AskUserQuestion, and rm/rmdir targeting a critical path), and the "Common setups" table notes that in a -p run the few calls that would still prompt are denied instead, with a container, VM, or sandbox runtime listed as required isolation.

stem: A platform team wants to ensure that Claude Code cannot execute certain destructive Bash commands across all developer workstations. Which approach provides the most robust and deterministic enforcement mechanism?

options.text: Configure a PreToolUse hook that evaluates the tool name and input, blocking the execution if a destructive command is detected.
Add instructions to the Claude Code system prompt explicitly forbidding the model from generating destructive commands.
Define an AgentRestriction policy in the Claude Code configuration file to disable the Bash tool for specific directories.
Modify the `.claudecodeignore` file to include all directories where destructive commands should be blocked.

explanation: Hooks in Claude Code, specifically PreToolUse hooks, allow developers to intercept and validate tool calls before they are executed. They provide a deterministic mechanism to enforce policies or block actions (such as exiting with a specific block code), making them the appropriate solution for robust security controls. By contrast, system prompts only provide soft guidance.

distractorNotes.b: System prompts provide "soft" guidance but do not deterministically guarantee that the model won't generate or attempt to run the command.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code does not feature an "AgentRestriction" policy in its configuration for directory-specific tool disabling.
distractorNotes.d: The `.claudecodeignore` file prevents Claude Code from reading or indexing specific files, but it does not intercept or block terminal commands.

sourceNote: Section "Exit code output": "exit code 2 is the only exit code that blocks through the code alone. Without valid JSON on stdout, Claude Code treats exit code 1 as a non-blocking error and proceeds with the action, even though 1 is the conventional Unix failure code. If your hook is meant to enforce a policy, use exit 2." The same section states "The blocking message is the reason from your JSON's blocking decision when it makes one, and your stderr text otherwise" and that for PreToolUse the block stops the tool call; the exit-code-0 subsection notes a hook "can deny the call, but staying silent doesn't approve it"; the timeouts subsection states a hook that reaches its timeout is cancelled with its output discarded. The worked example blocks on exit 0 by printing a PreToolUse permissionDecision of "deny" as JSON.

stem: A development team is integrating Claude Code into their Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline to automate routine codebase tasks. Which TWO capabilities represent foundational features of Claude Code's headless operation that enable this automation? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It can execute autonomously without requiring human interaction or interactive terminal approvals.
It requires a developer to authenticate via an interactive browser prompt during every pipeline run.
It can produce structured machine-readable output, such as JSON, for downstream pipeline steps to easily parse.
It relies on a desktop graphical interface to orchestrate background CI tasks.
It automatically bypasses all organizational repository security constraints when run in CI environments.

explanation: Claude Code can operate in a 'headless' mode designed for automated environments like CI/CD pipelines. In this mode, it executes autonomously without requiring human interaction or interactive approvals (such as workspace trust dialogs). To facilitate integration, it can output structured, machine-readable formats like JSON, allowing downstream pipeline steps to easily parse and utilize the response. Non-interactive authentication is natively supported via environment variables.

distractorNotes.b: In automated environments, Claude Code uses non-interactive authentication methods (like environment variables containing API keys) rather than requiring an interactive browser login on every run.
distractorNotes.d: Claude Code is a CLI tool and its headless operation does not require a desktop graphical interface.
distractorNotes.e: Claude Code does not bypass security constraints; it operates securely within the permissions granted to the credentials or environment it runs under.

sourceNote: Section "Start faster with bare mode": --bare skips "auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md", is "useful for CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine", and "In bare mode, Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain. For the Anthropic API, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment ... or supply an apiKeyHelper in the --settings JSON." The same section warns that without --bare, "a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json", with "no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt". Section "Get structured output": --output-format accepts text (default), json ("structured JSON with result, session ID, and metadata", "with the text result in the result field"), and stream-json, which is streamed using --verbose and --include-partial-messages.

stem: A developer added a convention to a project CLAUDE.md, but Claude Code seems to ignore it. Before rewriting the wording, what is the most direct way to find out whether the file was actually loaded into the session?

options.text: Run /compact and read its summary, since compaction lists every instruction file it re-reads.
Run /context and look for the file under the memory files part of the breakdown.
Run /permissions to confirm that reading the instruction file is allowed.
Delete the user configuration directory and restart, since a stale cache is the usual cause.

explanation: The /context command shows everything occupying the context window for the current session, broken down by category, including memory files, so it is the first check for whether an instruction file is present at all. If the file is missing there, the cause is location: instruction files load from the working directory and its parents at launch, while a CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory loads only on demand when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool. If /context shows the file did load, the problem is how the instruction is written, and the remedies are specificity, removing conflicting guidance, and keeping the file short. Targeted follow-ups are /memory, /skills, /hooks, /mcp, /permissions, /doctor, and /status, and a session started with customizations disabled isolates the surface responsible.

distractorNotes.a: Compaction summarizes the conversation to reclaim context. A project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk afterwards, but compaction reports no inventory of instruction files, so it answers nothing about what loaded at session start.
distractorNotes.c: Permission rules govern which tools Claude may use. They do not determine whether an instruction file is loaded into the session at startup.
distractorNotes.d: Deleting configuration is destructive and skips diagnosis. The documented isolation technique points a session at a separate, empty configuration directory instead of removing the real one.

sourceNote: Section "See what loaded into context": "The /context command shows everything occupying the context window for the current session, broken down by category: system prompt, system tools, MCP tools, custom subagents with the source each loaded from, memory files, skills, and conversation messages. Run it first to confirm whether your CLAUDE.md, rules, or skill descriptions are present at all." It adds that subdirectory CLAUDE.md files "load on demand when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool, not at session start", and that when the file did load, "the issue is likely how the instruction is written rather than whether it loaded". The follow-up command table lists /memory, /skills, /hooks, /mcp, /permissions, /doctor, and /status, and "Test against a clean configuration" describes pointing CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR at an empty directory. The compaction behavior is stated at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory: "Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction: after /compact, Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it into the session."

stem: A team wants Claude Code to run on every pull request in CI, with no engineer watching the run. Select TWO statements that correctly describe what running it non-interactively implies.

options.text: Non-interactive runs escalate their own permissions as needed, since blocking on a prompt that nobody can answer would deadlock the pipeline.
Because nobody is available to approve anything mid-run, the tools the run may use have to be settled before it starts rather than agreed as it goes.
The pipeline should decide the outcome by matching phrases in the printed transcript, because a programmatic run reports its status only in prose.
The run reports success or failure through its exit status, so the surrounding pipeline can branch on the outcome without reading the transcript.
Running without a terminal disables tool use altogether, so an automated run is limited to reading files and producing a written summary.

explanation: Removing the human from the loop changes two things at once. Every approval that a person would have given interactively has to be decided in advance, because there is nobody to ask once the run begins; that is a design decision about how much the run is trusted to do, made before it starts. And the surrounding automation needs a machine-readable verdict, which the process supplies through its exit status, so the pipeline can succeed or fail without anyone interpreting the output. Both follow from the absence of a person rather than from any particular invocation detail.

distractorNotes.a: Inverts the safety model. Self-escalation would mean an unattended run could grant itself anything it wanted, which is the opposite of what removing human oversight demands.
distractorNotes.c: Scraping prose for a verdict is brittle and unnecessary. It also throws away the reliable signal the process already provides for exactly this purpose.
distractorNotes.e: Non-interactive means no human prompts, not no tools. The run still edits files and executes commands, which is precisely why the permissions question matters.

sourceNote: Run Claude Code programmatically — non-interactive runs exit 0 on success and non-zero on failure so scripts can branch on exit status, and tools are auto-approved up front
